title: Simple graphs and vertex degrees
section: Graph Theory ▷ Vertices, Edges, and Degree

exposition.text:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of vertices and unordered pairs of distinct vertices
called edges, with no loops or repeated edges. Its order is the number n of vertices, and its

The complement of a simple graph on a fixed vertex set has exactly the missing edges; its de-
grees are n − 1 − deg(v). A regular graph has the same degree at every vertex. A degree sequence
is graphical if some simple graph realizes it. Loops and parallel edges violate simplicity, and in
their presence degree counts incidences, not just distinct neighbors.

question.text:
A simple graph has 12 vertices. Seven have degree 5 and the other five all have degree d. Which
value of d is impossible?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 5 (E) 7

solution.text:
The degree sum is 35 + 5d, which must be even. Thus d must be odd, excluding 4. The other
sequences are graphical; for example the Havel–Hakimi criterion confirms them. The parity
obstruction alone uniquely identifies the listed impossible value.

question.text:
A simple graph on eight vertices has six vertices of degree 5 and two of degree 4. How many
edges are missing from the complete graph?
(A) 7 (B) 8 (C) 9 (D) 10 (E) 11

solution.text:
The degree sum is 6(5)+2(4) = 38, so the graph has 19 edges. Since K has 28 edges, exactly

question.text:
Every finite simple graph with at least two vertices must have which property?
(A) A vertex of degree zero
(B) A vertex adjacent to all others
(C) Two vertices of equal degree
(D) An even number of vertices
(E) A connected complement

solution.text:
With n vertices, possible degrees are 0, 1, . . . , n − 1. But degrees zero and n − 1 cannot both
occur: a universal vertex would be adjacent to an allegedly isolated vertex. Thus n vertices
occupy at most n − 1 possible degrees, so the pigeonhole principle forces repetition.

question.text:
Which sequence cannot be the degrees of the vertices of a simple graph?
(A) (3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3) (B) (2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2)
(C) (4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4) (D) (5, 5, 3, 1, 1, 1)
(E) (5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)

solution.text:
The two vertices of degree five would each be adjacent to all other vertices, forcing every
other degree to be at least two. That contradicts the degrees one. The other sequences are
realized by K , a six-cycle, K minus a perfect matching, and a six-vertex star. An even

question.text:
A graph allows loops and parallel edges. At a vertex v there are two loops, three edges to w,
and one edge to u, where u, v, w are distinct. What are the degree of v and the number of dis-
tinct other vertices adjacent to v, respectively?
(A) (6, 2) (B) (8, 2) (C) (8, 3) (D) (4, 2) (E) (6, 3)

solution.text:
Each loop contributes two to the degree, each ordinary incident edge contributes one, and
parallel edges are counted separately. Thus the degree is 2 · 2 + 3 + 1 = 8. The distinct
other neighbors are only u, w, so there are two. Degree equals the number of neighbors only
under the simple-graph assumptions.
